case_study_insert.main_stem: Harbourview Seafoods (HVS) is a public limited company in the seafood-processing industry, based on the Atlantic coast and employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2008 by Derek Osei, it supplies frozen fillets to supermarket chains and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. HVS plans to invest $720,000 in a new cold-storage and filleting facility, financed by a $260,000 bank overdraft and $460,000 from a share issue. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $26, and produces 84,000 units a year. HVS faces fish-spoilage losses of 7% of catch and labour turnover of 11% among its processing staff.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The filleting line processed 19,800 cartons last quarter at a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.0% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 39 to 22 a month. Average delivery time to retailers was 3.1 days. A survey of 540 customers found 57% would pay $0.45 more for sustainably sourced fillets, and 51% check the origin label. Spoilage was 7% of catch. A skills audit shows 11 of 50 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new filleting machines; off-the-job training at the technical college costs $680 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harbourview Seafoods as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Seafood Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.00% to 5.75%, raising the cost of the $260,000 bank overdraft. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.60 to $14.39 an hour, increasing coastal processing payroll costs. (3) Diesel and ice input costs have risen 10.5% year-on-year, while consumer spending on frozen seafood grew 3.3%.

questions.question_text: HVS is funding its $720,000 cold-storage and filleting facility with a $260,000 bank overdraft and a $460,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for HVS of the share issue compared with the overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings in $460,000 that does not have to be repaid and carries no interest charge, unlike the $260,000 bank overdraft whose cost rises whenever the base rate moves. For a company with fixed costs of $240,000 a year and seasonal fish supplies, this protects liquidity while the facility is built, leaving more of the $26 selling price to cover the $14 variable cost.

Point 2: Equity does not carry the daily repayment pressure of an overdraft, so Derek Osei's new filleting facility cannot be threatened by a bank recall if catches fall below the 19,800 cartons processed last quarter. The share issue also spreads funding among investors instead of concentrating it on a 5.00% to 5.75% rate exposure; although existing shareholders dilute their control, the 57% of 540 surveyed customers willing to pay $0.45 more supports demand for the $720,000 expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to HVS's financing decision.

questions.question_text: HVS wants to promote its new sustainably sourced fillets while delivery times of 3.1 days persist. Consider a regional television campaign, local newspaper advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HVS choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Regional television: TV reaches a wide audience quickly and can show frozen fillets being prepared, supporting the 57% of 540 surveyed customers who would pay $0.45 more. Yet airtime is expensive for a company with $240,000 fixed costs and a $260,000 overdraft to service, and many viewers live too far from the Atlantic coast distribution network, so much of the spend is wasted.

Local newspaper advertising: Newspaper ads are cheaper and reach the immediate coastal catchment, which suits HVS supplying regional retailers, and coupons can fill slow days. Their limits are declining readership and a static image that cannot show the product or the 51% of customers who check origin labels, so they do little to build the premium sustainably sourced positioning.

Social media influencer marketing: Cooking and food influencers can show the fillets and the origin story to a large relevant audience and track engagement against the 19,800-carton baseline. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on credible partners, but cost per reached customer is low and the content can highlight the fall in complaints from 39 to 22, strengthening the sustainability message.

Recommendation: HVS should choose social media influencer marketing, backed by small local newspaper coupons. It demonstrates the product and origin credentials widely at lower cost than television and reaches beyond the newspaper's catchment. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a $720,000 facility funded partly by overdraft; newspapers alone are rejected as too passive to showcase a premium frozen product.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to HVS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HVS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and newspapers are rejected.

questions.question_text: HVS's labour turnover has reached 11% under autocratic leadership. Explain two benefits for HVS of changing to democratic leadership in its workforce of 50.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership would let the 50 employees, especially filleting operators, contribute ideas on spoilage control and shift patterns. Being consulted raises job satisfaction and commitment, which should reduce the 11% labour turnover that forces repeated hiring and retraining, and helps cut the 7% spoilage by drawing on the knowledge of staff who handle the catch daily.

Point 2: Involvement improves decisions because operators can flag defects before the 2.6% defect rate worsens, protecting the 57% of 540 customers willing to pay $0.45 more. Higher morale supports the 3.1-day delivery record to retailers, so the new $720,000 facility can run smoothly without the disruption of constantly replacing leavers under autocratic rules.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HVS's turnover, spoilage and expansion.

questions.question_text: HVS must train 11 of 50 staff who have not completed on-the-job training on the new filleting machines. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college. Which should HVS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the line is specific to HVS's own filleting machines and hygiene standards, costs no fees, and keeps the 11 trainees productive during the 19,800-carton quarter. It can directly target the 7% spoilage and the 2.6% defect rate because supervisors correct practice immediately. Weaknesses are that busy operators have less time to teach, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate for retailer audits.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $680 per employee costs 11 × $680 = $7,480, small beside the $720,000 investment. It provides structured, certified fish-hygiene skills and removes trainees from distractions. However, it pulls 11 of 50 staff off the line during peak processing, risking deliveries longer than the current 3.1 days, and generic content may not match HVS's exact equipment, requiring follow-up coaching.

Decision: HVS should choose on-the-job training as the main method, with short certified college modules later. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids worsening delivery times while 11% labour turnover already disrupts operations. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because lost shifts and the $7,480 fee would hit the 19,800-carton operation and the generic course would not cover the new filleting machines. A pilot with one shift should compare the 2.6% defect rate and 7% spoilage before HVS commits $7,480 to all 11 staff.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HVS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of HVS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HVS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: 84,000 − ($240,000 ÷ ($26.00 − $14.00)) = 84,000 − 20,000 = 64,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 64,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $26.00 − $14.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HVS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. A margin of safety of 64,000 cartons against output of 84,000 shows HVS can absorb a large fall in catches and still cover $240,000 fixed costs, guiding how fast to fill the $720,000 cold store.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 lets managers test a retailer discount: cutting the $26.00 price by $2 to $24.00 leaves $10.00 contribution, so they can judge whether extra volume offsets the loss before answering the 39 monthly complaints about value.
3. With fixed costs of $240,000 and $12.00 contribution, break-even is $240,000 ÷ $12.00 = 20,000 cartons, a target for the new facility beyond the 19,800 cartons processed last quarter.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost, $240,000 ÷ 84,000 = $2.86 plus $14.00 = $16.86 a carton, against the $680 training fee and 7% spoilage to see whether better training lowers costs.

questions.model_answer: (i) Margin of safety = 64,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 64,000-carton cushion above break-even; discount pricing from $26.00 against $12.00 contribution; 20,000-carton target for the new facility; and unit-cost benchmarking at $16.86 against $680 training and 7% spoilage.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HVS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HVS's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.69 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.94 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $75,000 trade receivables + $38,000 cash = $203,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $95,000 + $62,000 = $227,000. For 2024, $203,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.69 and ($203,000 − $90,000) ÷ $120,000 = $113,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.94. For 2025, $227,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.75 and ($227,000 − $70,000) ÷ $130,000 = $157,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.21.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved on both measures. The first ratio rose from 1.69 to 1.75 even though current liabilities increased from $120,000 to $130,000, because current assets grew faster, helped by cash rising from $38,000 to $62,000. The second measure climbed from 0.94 to 1.21 and is the more useful signal for a seasonal processor: it shows HVS could meet bills without relying on selling $70,000 of frozen stock, valuable while a $260,000 overdraft and a $720,000 facility are outstanding. The reservation is trade receivables, up from $75,000 to $95,000, which lock away cash if supermarket customers pay late, especially with 11% labour turnover adding costs.

Conclusion: HVS's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the gain is not driven by inventory, so short-term solvency is stronger. Rising receivables remain the main risk, so credit control should be tightened as the new facility starts up.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: HVS is considering a loyalty scheme for retailers buying its sustainably sourced fillets. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HVS of this approach.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A loyalty scheme rewards retailers and supports the 57% of 540 surveyed customers who would pay $0.45 more, encouraging repeat orders that lift the 19,800-carton baseline without heavy advertising. More cartons spread the $240,000 fixed costs and protect the $12.00 contribution against 10.5% diesel and ice inflation, helping the $720,000 facility break even sooner.

Disadvantage: Rewards cut the $26.00 selling price and therefore the $12.00 contribution on rewarded cartons, and tracking software adds to fixed costs while a $260,000 overdraft is outstanding. The insert gives no redemption or setup figure, so the net effect cannot be quantified. If rewards are too small they will not change retailer behaviour, so HVS should trial the scheme with one customer group and compare orders with the 540-customer survey first.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HVS's survey, cartons, costs and overdraft.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in diesel and ice input costs will affect HVS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.00% to 5.75%): An overdraft is variable-rate, so if the $260,000 overdraft is fully drawn the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $260,000 = $1,950 a year (0.0075 × $260,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $240,000, but the cost is immediate rather than deferred. The rise may also discourage some discretionary seafood spending despite the 3.3% growth in frozen-seafood demand.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.39 an hour): HVS's workforce of 50 includes many hourly-paid processing staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 84,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 1,680 cartons per worker, so the higher wage is sustainable only if throughput holds; cutting the 11% turnover and the 7% spoilage would help protect that rate.

Input cost inflation (10.5%): Diesel and ice feed the $14.00 variable cost on every carton. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $14.00 were exposed, 10.5% × $14.00 = $1.47 a carton, and at 84,000 cartons that is roughly $123,480 a year (84,000 × $1.47). Even a smaller exposed share erodes the $12.00 contribution on each carton, and the effect recurs with every unit unlike a one-off interest figure.

Conclusion: The 10.5% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across 84,000 cartons and directly attacks the $12.00 contribution that funds the $720,000 facility and the overdraft, whereas the overdraft costs $1,950 a year on the stated balance and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 1,680 cartons per worker. HVS should cut the 7% spoilage and review the $26.00 price rather than absorb the whole rise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to HVS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HVS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
